sections.title: What is Binary Search on Answer?
sections.content:
**Binary search on answer** - also called **parametric search** - applies binary search not to find an element in a sorted array, but to find the optimal value of an answer that satisfies some monotone condition. The pattern: 'find the minimum X such that `feasible(X)` is true' or 'find the maximum X such that `feasible(X)` is true.' If you can write a boolean function `feasible(mid)` that checks whether answer `mid` is achievable, and if the feasibility is **monotone** (once true, stays true for all larger or smaller values), you can binary search on `mid` over the answer range.

The answer space is typically: minimum days, minimum capacity, minimum speed, minimum largest sum, maximum minimum distance, minimum number of groups. These don't look like search problems - they look like optimization problems. The insight is that the answer itself lies on a number line where the feasibility flips from false to true (or true to false) exactly once, forming a sorted boolean sequence like `[false, false, false, true, true, true]`. Binary search finds that boundary in O(log(answerRange)) calls to `feasible`.

This pattern is one of the most commonly missed on hard LeetCode problems. Students recognize binary search on a sorted array (straightforward), but don't recognize when the answer space is implicitly sorted. The signals are: the problem asks for minimum/maximum of something, the constraint involves distributing n items across k groups, the problem involves capacity or speed or time, and a brute force would try each candidate answer linearly. When each linear check is O(n) and the answer range spans up to 10^9, binary search on answer drops the total complexity from O(n × answerRange) to O(n × log(answerRange)).

The hardest part is writing the `feasible` function correctly and proving monotonicity. Once those are done, the binary search shell is mechanical. The easiest way to verify monotonicity: if `feasible(mid)` is true, would making `mid` larger (for minimize) or smaller (for maximize) keep it true? If yes, you have monotonicity and the pattern applies.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use binary search on answer when the problem asks for the minimum or maximum of a parameter, a `feasible(mid)` check function is natural to write, and feasibility is monotone. The key test: can you write a greedy or simulation `feasible(mid)` in O(n) or O(n log n)? If yes and the answer range is large, binary search on answer is almost certainly the intended solution.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## The Feasible Function and Monotonicity

The hardest part of this pattern is writing `feasible(mid)` correctly. It asks: 'if the answer were `mid`, can we satisfy all constraints?'

**Koko Eating Bananas**: if Koko eats `mid` bananas/hour, can she finish all piles in `h` hours? `feasible(mid) = sum(ceil(pile / mid) for each pile) <= h`. Monotonicity: if she can finish at speed `mid`, she can definitely finish at speed `mid+1`. So feasibility is monotonically non-decreasing - binary search finds the minimum speed where it flips to true.

**Ship Packages**: if ship capacity is `mid`, can all packages be shipped in `d` days? Greedily pack packages left to right, starting a new day when adding the next package would exceed `mid`. `feasible(mid)` = number of days needed <= d.

## Setting the Search Boundaries

The binary search range `[lo, hi]` must cover all possible answers without missing the correct one.

- **Koko Eating Bananas**: `lo = 1` (must eat at least 1), `hi = max(piles)` (eating the whole largest pile in one hour is the maximum needed speed).
- **Ship Packages in D Days**: `lo = max(weights)` (must fit the heaviest package), `hi = sum(weights)` (carry all in one trip).
- **Split Array Largest Sum**: `lo = max(arr)` (each part must hold at least the largest element), `hi = sum(arr)` (all in one part).

Setting lo too high or hi too low means the correct answer is outside the search range - always reason about the absolute minimum and maximum plausible answer.

## Minimize vs Maximize Template

**Minimize** (find minimum mid where feasible is true): when `feasible(mid)` is true, record mid as a candidate and search left (`hi = mid - 1`); when false, search right (`lo = mid + 1`). Return the last recorded candidate.

**Maximize** (find maximum mid where feasible is true): when `feasible(mid)` is true, record mid and search right (`lo = mid + 1`); when false, search left (`hi = mid - 1`). Return the last recorded candidate.

The difference is which direction you explore when feasibility holds.

## Recognizing the Pattern

Phrases that signal binary search on answer: 'minimum capacity/speed/days such that...', 'maximum minimum distance', 'split array into k parts to minimize the largest part', 'minimum number of X to accomplish Y'. The key test: does making the parameter larger monotonically make feasibility easier (or harder)? If the answer is yes to one of these, binary search on answer applies.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Binary search over the answer space [lo, hi]. When feasible(mid) is true, record mid and shrink right (try smaller); when false, expand left (need larger). Returns the minimum feasible value.

items.name: Maximize Minimum Distance
items.description: Find the maximum distance such that you can place k elements with at least that distance apart. feasible(mid) checks greedily whether k elements fit with minimum gap = mid. Search direction is reversed: search right when feasible (maximize).

items.name: Split Array Largest Sum
items.description: Split array into k subarrays minimizing the largest subarray sum. feasible(mid) greedily checks whether the array can be split into at most k parts each with sum <= mid. lo = max(arr), hi = sum(arr).

items.name: Koko Eating Bananas
items.description: Minimize eating speed such that all piles can be finished in h hours. feasible(mid) sums ceil(pile/mid) for each pile and checks if the total hours <= h. Classic minimize-template example.

items.name: Minimize Maximum of Array
items.description: Binary search on the maximum value achievable after applying allowed operations to the array. feasible(mid) checks whether all elements can be reduced to <= mid under the operation constraints using a greedy left-to-right pass.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.explanation: Binary search runs O(log(answerRange)) iterations - for typical problems with answer range up to 10^9, that's at most 30 iterations. Each iteration runs feasible(mid) which is O(n) for a greedy scan. Total: O(n log(answerRange)). Space is O(1) beyond the input - no auxiliary structures needed for the binary search shell itself.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Wrong lo/hi bounds - if lo is above the correct answer or hi is below it, the answer is never found and the binary search converges to an incorrect boundary; always reason through what makes the absolute minimum plausible answer (lo) and absolute maximum (hi) before coding.

Feasible function not actually monotone - binary search on answer only works when feasibility flips exactly once across the answer range; if feasible(mid) can be true, then false, then true again, binary search converges on the wrong boundary; always verify monotonicity before applying.

Minimize vs maximize confusion - for minimize problems explore left when feasible (set hi = mid - 1); for maximize problems explore right when feasible (set lo = mid + 1); mixing these causes the binary search to converge on the opposite boundary, returning the worst feasible value instead of the optimal one.

Integer overflow in mid calculation - `mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)` is safe in JavaScript but overflows 32-bit integers in other languages for large bounds; prefer `lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2)` as a portable habit.

Off-by-one in feasible function for greedy packing - in 'ship packages in D days', the greedy packing must count the final partial group after the loop ends; counting days only when a new day starts (capacity exceeded) and forgetting to add 1 for the last group makes feasible return true when it should return false, converging on a value one step too small.

items.title: Koko Eating Bananas
items.why: The canonical minimize-template problem - tests writing feasible(speed) as a sum of ceil(pile/speed) and correctly setting lo/hi bounds.

items.title: Split Array Largest Sum
items.why: Tests the greedy feasible check (can we split into k parts each <= mid?) and recognizing that lo = max(arr) is required because a single element can't be split further.

items.title: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls
items.why: Tests the maximize variant - search right when feasible, record ans and try larger - and the greedy feasibility check for minimum-gap placement.

items.title: Minimize Maximum of Array
items.why: Tests identifying that the answer space is monotone and writing a greedy feasible check that verifies whether all elements can be reduced to <= mid under the given constraints.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Binary search on answer searches a linear answer space using halving. Binary lifting for LCA applies the same power-of-2 halving idea to trees - building a table of 2^j-th ancestors and using binary decomposition to answer ancestor and LCA queries in O(log n).
